title: Palantir Stock Could Finish 2026 Lower. Its Only 2 Losing Years Ended Very Differently.
detail:
Palantir Stock Could Finish 2026 Lower. Its Only 2 Losing Years Ended Very Differently.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:57 AM MST 5 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) has finished only two calendar years in the red since it started trading in September 2020, and it might add a third. As I write, shares are near $160, about 10% under the $177.75 they closed at to end 2025, with less than six weeks of trading left in the year.

The stock has already swung widely this year, closing as low as about $107 in late June before reaching a record close over $209 in October.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Palantir's two losing years didn't end the same way, though. The stock dropped around 23% in 2021 and then shed another 65% in 2022. But the 2022 loss was followed by a 167% rise in 2023.

What separated the two? I think it mainly boiled down to the price investors were paying heading into the next year, and whether the business was getting stronger. On one of those two fronts, today looks more like the end of 2021 than the end of 2022.

Image source: Getty Images.

A pricey slowdown

Palantir's 2021 wasn't a bad year for the business. Revenue climbed 41% year over year to $1.54 billion, and the company's net loss shrank to $520 million from $1.17 billion in 2020.

But growth was cooling as the year ended. Fourth-quarter revenue grew 34% year over year, a slowdown from the full year's pace.

The stock wasn't cheap, either, even after its 2021 drop. Based on Palantir's share count at the end of 2021, its $18.21 closing price gave the company a market cap of around $37 billion -- about 24 times its 2021 sales.

Sure, a high price can hold up if growth does, but Palantir's growth kept cooling. Full-year revenue grew 24% in 2022, and fourth-quarter revenue climbed just 18% year over year. The company also lost $374 million that year, and the stock shed around two-thirds of its value.

A cheap stock turns a profit

The end of 2022 set up something very different. At $6.42 a share, Palantir's market cap was around $13.5 billion. Put another way, investors were paying around 7 times sales, based on 2022 revenue of $1.91 billion.

Then, in February 2023, Palantir posted its first quarter of positive GAAP net income, earning $31 million in the fourth quarter of 2022. Management also said it expected GAAP net income for all of 2023.

Interestingly, the business didn't speed up in 2023. Revenue rose just 17% to $2.23 billion, slower than in either losing year. But net income swung to $210 million, from the $374 million loss in 2022.

title: UiPath vs. Palantir Technologies: Which AI Automation Platform Makes a Better Stock Buy for 2027?

UiPath vs. Palantir Technologies: Which AI Automation Platform Makes a Better Stock Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:33 AM MST 7 min read

PLTR

Trading disclosure

Artificial intelligence is reshaping the corporate world, forcing investors to choose which software giants will lead the next decade. Comparing UiPath (NYSE:PATH) and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) reveals two distinct paths to growth.

UiPath focuses on robotic process automation to handle routine work, while Palantir Technologies provides advanced data analytics and decision-making platforms. They are often compared because both leverage artificial intelligence to enhance productivity for large organizations. Understanding their different growth stages and valuation levels is key for any investor looking toward 2027.

The case for UiPath

UiPath provides an automation platform designed to help organizations run more efficiently by orchestrating AI, robots, and people. The company operates among tech stocks focused on enterprise productivity. It serves roughly 10,747 customers across sectors like finance and healthcare.

The business relies heavily on its top-tier clients, including 357 customers with annual recurring revenue of $1 million or more. Strategic alliances with partners like Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) are vital for expanding its market reach. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached approximately $1.7 billion. This represents a revenue growth of roughly 15% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net income of about $361.9 million for this same interval, resulting in a net margin of about 21%.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 2.5x. This figure indicates the company's ability to meet its short-term obligations using its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, comparing total debt to total shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow reached about $352.2 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 78.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Palantir Technologies

Palantir Technologies builds software platforms for integrating and analyzing data for human-driven decision-making. It serves a diverse range of public institutions and commercial enterprises, including a significant engagement with the U.S. Army. The company manages strategic partnerships with global entities like SOMPO Holdings (OTC:NHOLF) to support its implementation services.

Revenue concentration is a factor for the business, as its top three customers accounted for roughly 16% of revenue in 2025. This reliance on a small number of high-value contracts can lead to volatility if major projects are delayed. However, the company continues to expand its reach through joint ventures and global system integrators.

Key Takeaways

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 17 bought Palantir, Stanley Druckenmiller's family office among them, and 6 sold.

GQG Partners made the biggest buy, a new stake worth $955 million at quarter-end prices, while three of the six sellers bought or added to Costco in the same quarter.

Palantir is down 23% since Sept. 30, but analysts expect its earnings to more than double from 2026 to 2028, and its forward P/E of 62x sits well below its five-year average of 102x.

On those numbers the buyers have the better case, and the bookings in Palantir's fourth-quarter report, expected in early February, are the next test.

Big money couldn't agree on Palantir (PLTR:NASDAQ) last quarter. Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30 (funds readers know, or ones with $1 billion or more of US stocks, leaving out quant and index funds), 17 bought it, by opening a position or adding 20% or more, and 6 sold out or cut 20% or more. In all, 39 of them held it on Sept. 30.

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office was one of the buyers. And so far, the sellers look smarter: Palantir is down 23% since Sept. 30, while Costco Wholesale (COST:NASDAQ), which three of the six sellers bought or added to in the same quarter, is up 21%. A 13F doesn't show when anyone traded or what they paid, so those are just each stock's moves from its Sept. 30 close.

GQG Partners, which manages $164 billion, opened a 5.10 million-share stake worth $955 million at quarter-end prices, per its 13F filed Nov. 13. That's 1.8% of its 13F stocks. Druckenmiller's position is far smaller: 80,100 shares worth $15 million, or 0.4% of the $4.15 billion of US stocks in his family office's 13F, filed Nov. 16. It's his 41st-largest of 60 positions.

The sellers cut deep

Blue Sparrow, whose 13F holds $8.3 billion of US stocks, cut its stake 69%, from 1.24 million shares to 383,700. At quarter-end prices, the shares it sold were worth about $159 million. Hyperion Asset Management, which manages $9.7 billion, cut 42% to 647,697 shares, about $87 million's worth. Palantir is still 3.3% of Hyperion's 13F stocks, a bigger share than at GQG or Sands. Funds run by Cathie Wood's Ark Invest sold 58,339 shares in Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) on Nov. 12, worth about $10 million at the day's close of $171.58. Ark's flagship fund sold 53,547 of the shares, and its internet-focused fund sold the other 4,792.

The artificial intelligence (AI) software company's stock has kept dropping since. As I write, Palantir trades near $157, about 9% below where Ark sold and about 25% below its Oct. 9 record close of $209.05.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

A big growth investor selling into a slide can look like a vote against the stock. But I don't think that particular sale says much. And the fall since then has sent shares well below the buy price of around $172 I set for Palantir earlier this month.

Cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

A small trim

Ark trades its Palantir stake often, and in both directions. It sold around $9.6 million of the stock in three days from Oct. 19 through Oct. 21. Then on Nov. 3, the day after Palantir's third-quarter results, Ark bought 63,638 shares across five funds, worth around $11.2 million at that day's close of $175.40.

So, the Nov. 12 sale mostly undid a purchase Ark made just after earnings. Four days later, though, Ark's robotics-focused fund sold around $16 million of the stock. Counting every November trade through Nov. 16, Ark has sold more Palantir shares than it bought this month.

The stake is still big, too. As of Nov. 18, Ark's flagship fund owned around 2.1 million Palantir shares, worth about $325 million, according to Ark's daily holdings file. The flagship fund's 53,547-share sale on Nov. 12 was under 3% of that.

Palantir keeps raising its forecast

Showing how consistently the company has topped its own forecasts, Palantir's third-quarter revenue climbed 96% year over year to around $2.31 billion, about 7% above the midpoint of the guidance management gave in August. It had done that twice already this year. First-quarter revenue was around 6% above the guidance midpoint, and second-quarter revenue about 8% above it. And every report brought a higher full-year outlook. Palantir's 2026 revenue guidance began the year at around $7.19 billion. It's now around $8.53 billion, up about 19%, which would mean growth of 91% over 2025.

The firm also raised its forecast for U.S. commercial revenue (sales to American businesses) to at least $3.56 billion, which would be growth of at least 143%.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock lost 23.8% between October 21 and November 19, 2026, while the S&P 500 fell 7.4%. You probably still think of Palantir as a government software company, but its latest quarter tells a different story. In that quarter, which ended September 30, sales to U.S. companies surpassed those to the U.S. government for the first time. Yet the stock has dropped, and that is the contradiction. So how big has Palantir's business with U.S. companies become?

Palantir Now Sells More To U.S. Companies Than Government

In the third quarter of 2026, Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier. Sales to the U.S. government rose 96% to $953 million. Sales to U.S. companies are now the larger of the two U.S. businesses, and they are growing faster.

Palantir's sales to U.S. businesses grew 148% in a year, and its shares still dropped 23.8% in a month. When a big part of your savings sits in a single stock, a drop like that is hard to sleep through. Instead of one company, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio owns 30 quality companies in equal amounts, and it is up more than 105% since September 2020. Look inside HQ.

A year earlier, in the third quarter of 2025, Palantir recorded $397 million in U.S. commercial revenue. That means it added $587 million of quarterly sales from U.S. companies in one year. The customer base expanded as well. Palantir had 686 U.S. commercial customers at the end of the quarter, 29% more than a year earlier. Management said demand for its Sovereign AI offering is speeding up this business.

What Are You Paying For Palantir's Growth?

For anyone looking at the stock, the price is the obvious worry. Even after the recent drop, Palantir traded at 100.8 times its earnings over the past twelve months at the November 19 close. The S&P 500 traded at 21.5 times.

Palantir answers that worry with its U.S. commercial business. Management raised its 2026 forecast for U.S. commercial revenue to more than $3.559 billion, which would represent growth of at least 143% for the year. The company expects its total 2026 revenue to grow 91%, so U.S. commercial sales are forecast to grow faster than the company as a whole. Both figures are forecasts rather than results, and at this price a slowdown in that growth would hurt.

What Could Go Wrong For Palantir's Commercial Push?

New contracts present a weak spot. In the third quarter, the total value of new U.S. commercial contracts Palantir signed was $1.463 billion, up 11% from a year earlier. That pace is far slower than the 148% rise in U.S. commercial revenue. Management said several large deals were shorter than usual, and it expects contracts to grow longer and larger over time.

Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.

Over the past month, shares of this company have returned -21.7%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -6.6% change. During this period, the Zacks Internet - Software industry, which Palantir Technologies falls in, has lost 13.3%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

After five decades in the investment business, billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller is having a particularly difficult time figuring out where the market is headed. And he's decided he'd rather sit on the sidelines than get it wrong.

"We're trying to not lose money, as opposed to make money," he said during an interview at the TomorrowX Summit (1) in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 17.

Top Picks

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

A day earlier, his family office, Duquesne, disclosed that it had dumped its entire stake in Google's parent company, Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), during the third quarter of 2026. Among its new investments were stakes in three gold mining companies worth a combined $129.1 million at the end of September.

For a man who went three decades at Duquesne Capital without a losing year (2), the decision to pull back is worth noting.

And if you're hoping to retire in the next few years, you may have more in common with Druckenmiller than you'd think. After decades of building wealth, protecting what you've accumulated can become more pressing than chasing another year of impressive returns.

Why Druckenmiller is backing away from stocks

In January, Druckenmiller thought a recession in the following six to 12 months was almost impossible.

The economy was strong, the Federal Reserve was expected to continue cutting interest rates and the market rally extended beyond a handful of technology stocks. Copper prices were climbing, suggesting healthy demand for a metal used in everything from home construction to data centers.

When asked how much of the portfolio he held in January he still owns today, Druckenmiller's response was simple: "Basically, almost none."

Many of the economic signals that informed his outlook have since reversed.

The Fed is no longer cutting interest rates and credit spreads have widened, meaning investors are demanding more compensation for taking on credit risk. At the same time, defensive stocks, such as those of companies that sell essential goods and services, have started outperforming companies whose fortunes are more closely tied to economic growth.
